channel.title: Ayiti Sitwayen · Candidates under scrutiny
channel.description: Understand the record, follow the money and examine documented connections. Each article follows one question in plain language.

item.title: Marc Arthur Drouillard: what a 2016 footnote adds to the small vote total
item.description: An old result does not explain an alliance. The observers’ report adds another piece.

item.title: Jacky Lumarque in 2015: do not merge two clearance files
item.description: A candidate’s name on a decision does not mean it covers every previous role.

item.title: Jacky Lumarque: the vocational-training test starts before the campaign
item.description: An education career supplies experience to examine, not results to assume.

item.title: Olivier Barrau’s youth corps: who selects and who pays?
item.description: A foundation event differs from a national service that must serve all citizens.

item.title: Olivier Barrau and AIC: the IDB’s $2 million was not a campaign gift
item.description: The 2012 loan record identifies a specific financial relationship and purpose to examine.

item.title: Olivier Barrau: from a family insurance business to presidential ambition
item.description: A business history can explain a career. It cannot replace an account of financial interests.

item.title: Etzer Emile’s school budget: 16% and 22% measure different things
item.description: Money authorized on paper does not always equal money delivered to a service.

item.title: Etzer Emile: 5,000 small projects mean 5 billion gourdes
item.description: The arithmetic is simple. Choosing beneficiaries fairly is the harder test.

item.title: Etzer Emile: 500 megawatts does not explain the electricity bill
item.description: To assess the promise, follow power from the plant to the household.

item.title: Etzer Emile’s $30 billion plan: who provides the money?
item.description: A total shows the scale of a promise. Funding sources show who carries the risk.

item.title: Etzer Emile wants to double the police. When will recruits be ready?
item.description: Announcing training and putting a prepared officer on the street are different steps.

item.title: Privert and Canada: what does the sanctions record establish?
item.description: The list confirms an administrative designation. It does not replace evidence about each alleged act.

item.title: Muscadin: public protection and the 76 cases documented by the UN
item.description: Support for a security official and evidence about his methods are different questions.

item.title: Gary Bodeau: when an appointment vote allegedly had a price
item.description: The U.S. Treasury describes payments intended to influence votes in the Chamber of Deputies. Bodeau disputes the allegations.

item.title: What Martelly’s lobbying contract asks Washington to change
item.description: The document targets sanctions policy. It is neither a verdict nor a promise of success.

item.title: Martelly’s lobbying file: who is paying?
item.description: A U.S. filing reports $75,000 received; the contract specifies other amounts. Those are different facts.

item.title: 54 Palace rifles: where a family connection meets public responsibility
item.description: The UN report names a security official and a family connection. The public role and the weapons trail must be examined together.

item.title: Martelly and gangs: what the UN report says about intermediaries
item.description: The 2023 report describes money, weapons and people connecting them. Each link needs its own evidence.

item.title: Martelly: what do the three U.S. restrictions cover?
item.description: The word “sanctions” covers specific measures. Their actual terms matter.

item.title: After Martelly’s school promise, demand clear accounts
item.description: Our editorial position: a promise to serve children should include a way for the public to check each stage of the money trail.

item.title: Claude Joseph and the Moïse case: what changed after 2024
item.description: Understanding the case requires following Haiti’s inquiry and the U.S. prosecutions separately, including what happened after the first accusations.

item.title: School-fee money: the accounting problem continued
item.description: A report covering 2023–2024 says FNE revenue was counted in the government budget balance while its spending was left out. Why does that matter?

item.title: Martelly and Privert: what did the school-fee lawsuit allege?
item.description: A group of U.S. residents challenged the transfer and call charges. Here are their allegations, the court’s response and the limits of the evidence.

item.title: Martelly and the $1.50 fee: what were families paying for?
item.description: Under Martelly, a transfer fee became part of a promise of free schooling. A lawsuit later challenged how the arrangement worked.
